GUIDE.label: A Researcher's Guide to Combustion Science (NASA, 2015)

PSI-TABLES.label: NASA PSI experimental tables (CC0): PSI-69 FLEX and PSI-25 BASS-II. Values computed by JaPax from the recorded rows.

CHALLENGE.label: Official challenge statement: Flame in Freefall (NASA Space Apps 2026)

fuels: C2H4/N2 on 25 mm and 50 mm porous burners

conditions.note: Habitat atmospheres considered by NASA, as stated in the PSI objectives.

investigations.summary: A gas burner that emulates how solid materials burn in a still atmosphere, tested in the atmospheres planned for spacecraft and bases.

findings.text: Quasi-steady burning of condensed-phase materials such as PMMA and Nylon was observed in microgravity with NO air flow, notably in the oxygen-enriched atmospheres being considered for future spacecraft; at 21% O2 such flames self-extinguished in a short time.
Cutting ventilation is an established step to put out spacecraft fires; these results suggest it may not be enough in oxygen-rich atmospheres.
The authors suggest NASA may want to make more use of its alternative flammability Test 2 (cone calorimeter), which can measure material properties matching the microgravity flames seen with BRE.

investigations.spaceApp: Material selection and fire-response protocols for lunar habitat atmospheres.

fuels: PMMA (flat samples and 1 cm and 2 cm spheres)

conditions.note: 41 samples and 89 test points. The O2 range is not given in the fact sheet. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

investigations.summary: Burns solid samples in a controlled-flow duct inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox and extinguishes the flame by ramping up a nitrogen flow.

findings.text: Recent BASS results indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is NOT conservative: materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
Local application of suppressant is not adequate for extinguishment: the local jet entrains air and sustains the flame even when the ambient airflow is turned off.
Hypothesis: with adequate ventilation, materials in microgravity burn as well if not better than in normal gravity under otherwise identical conditions.

investigations.spaceApp: NASA's spacecraft materials selection relies on a 1-g standard test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) that ignores low-gravity effects.
investigations.earthApp: Validates combustion models used for terrestrial problems.

fuels: rods, spherical sections, slabs, films and fabric sheets (thicker, more realistic geometries)

conditions.note: O2 is the MEASURED initial O2 range (13.6–22.2 % by volume) across the 129 tests in the PSI-25 table. Primary variables per PSI: flow velocity and direction, ambient oxygen (via nitrogen dilution) and sample geometry. Airflow units are not stated in the table.

investigations.summary: Follow-up to BASS with thicker, more realistic fuels; it bridges the 1-g Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity.

findings.text: Objective: study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows, and give SoFIE investigators preliminary data.
Helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future missions.
None of the 129 recorded tests started at 26.5% O2 or more (initial O2 ranged from 13.6% to 22.2%): there is no BASS-II solid-material data at lunar-habitat oxygen levels.

investigations.spaceApp: Material selection and extinguishment methods for missions far from Earth.
investigations.earthApp: Models applicable to wildfires and building fires.

conditions.note: O2 and pressure are MEASURED ranges across the 274 tests in the PSI-69 table (pressures cluster at 0.70, 1.0, 2.0, 2.7 and 3.05 atm). The fact sheet planned O2 0.10–0.50 and 0.5–1.0 atm. The main diluent is N2, with a few tests using He.

investigations.summary: Burns fuel droplets in mixtures of oxygen and diluents to map flammability limits and the effectiveness of inert suppressants (CO2, He).

findings.text: The flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity; terrestrial standards for inert-gas suppressants do not offer the same margin of safety in low gravity.
Demonstrated radiative and diffusive extinction, combustion instabilities, lower flammability limits and explained the cool-flame phenomenon after visible flame extinction.
Low pressures are tested because one extinguishing strategy is to isolate the habitat and vent the cabin to space.

Of the 274 recorded tests, 186 ended in extinction, 61 in disruption and 27 in completion. At lunar-habitat-like conditions (0.6–0.8 atm and O2 ≥ 26.5%) there are 17 tests and none ended in extinction (15 disruption, 2 completion).

investigations.spaceApp: Provides the most conservative estimate of the limiting oxygen index (LOI) for steady combustion.
investigations.earthApp: Heptane and methanol models are building blocks for practical fuels such as diesel and jet fuel.

conditions.note: 30 to 60 tests per group (pure, mixtures, convective flow, droplet pairs). The guide shows ethanol at 30% O2 and 2.4 atm in a soot example.

investigations.summary: Successor to FLEX: studies slow convective flows, droplet-droplet interactions and more complex fuels.

findings.text: Four experiment groups: pure fuels, fuel mixtures, convective flow and binary droplet arrays, with 30 to 60 tests each.
Includes international variants: FLEX-2J (JAXA, flame spread along droplet arrays) and FLEX-ICE-GA (biofuels, Italian CNR).

investigations.earthApp: Verifies models of real transportation and industrial fuels.

conditions.note: Includes the effect of helium dilution on cool flames.

sensors: UV camera (OH* emission and flame size)
investigations.summary: Studies cool flames (low-temperature combustion) in fuel droplets as a function of pressure, droplet size and helium dilution.

findings.text: A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition of practical fuels and fuel additives, and for designing advanced engines.
Investigates the relationship between droplet size, pressure and flame extinction, and the consequences of soot formation during cool-flame combustion.

investigations.spaceApp: Cool flames are a candidate safety concern (persistence after the visible flame goes out); their effect on detection is NOT verified in the sources.
investigations.earthApp: Design of cleaner fuels and engines.

conditions.note: The challenge statement says an O2-N2 mixture of up to 85% O2 flowed from a spherical burner, creating an inside-out flame.

investigations.summary: Determines the conditions under which cool diffusion flames exist on spherical porous burners; the microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentration.

findings.text: Hypothesis: testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate, for the first time, steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners with propane, n-butane and n-pentane.
Contains the microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations (up to 85%).

investigations.spaceApp: Data at extreme O2 conditions, relevant to habitat and spacesuit atmospheres.
investigations.earthApp: Improves the efficiency of internal combustion engines.

conditions.note: Soot-inception limits as a function of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert and pressure.

investigations.summary: Measures soot inception and structure of spherical diffusion flames in microgravity.

findings.text: Hypothesis: microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first drops below about 1130 K.

investigations.earthApp: Helps improve efficiency and reduce emissions in terrestrial combustors.

conditions.note: Weak coflow diffusion flames as a function of velocity and fuel dilution. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

sensors: thin-filament pyrometry (flame temperature in non-sooting regions)
investigations.summary: Benchmark data on coflow diffusion flames to test computational models at the extremes of fuel dilution.

findings.text: Characterizes flame shape, lift-off height, temperatures and extinction limits, and the sooting tendency with long residence times.

investigations.earthApp: Diffusion flames are the flame type in most practical combustion devices.

conditions.note: The challenge statement says the electric field mimics partial gravity through its effect on the ions in the flame. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

investigations.summary: Studies how an electric field changes laminar diffusion flames; the challenge statement cites it as a way to mimic partial gravity.

findings.text: Per the challenge statement, the electric field acts on the ions naturally present in flames and mimics partial gravity.
PSI clarifies it is not conducted for space applications, although findings could aid future space combustion devices (e.g., solid waste processing).

investigations.spaceApp: Not designed for space applications, but PSI notes the findings could aid future space-based combustion devices (e.g. solid waste processing).
investigations.earthApp: Electric fields can reduce harmful pollutants and soot and may allow more efficient combustion, cutting fuel use and emissions.

conditions.note: Uncrewed experiment aboard the Cygnus cargo vehicle. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

sensors: solid-state sensors (pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction)
investigations.summary: A large-scale fire deliberately set aboard an uncrewed cargo vehicle to study how a realistic fire grows in low gravity.

findings.text: Determines microgravity flammability limits of several spacecraft materials and helps validate NASA's material selection criteria.
Hypothesis: using terrestrial fires and standards to design spacecraft fire safety carries an inherent risk because of the uncertainty.

investigations.spaceApp: A realistic fire on an exploration vehicle with no risk to a crew.
investigations.earthApp: Benefits fire safety in mines, aircraft and submarines.

conditions.note: Same objectives as Saffire-I. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

sensors: solid-state sensors (pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction)
investigations.summary: Second Saffire flight, in the Cygnus pressurized cargo module.

findings.text: Same objectives: how fast a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and low-g flammability limits compared with NASA's normal-gravity screening test.

investigations.spaceApp: A realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which is too risky to test crewed. Results set microgravity flammability limits for spacecraft materials and help validate NASA's material-selection criteria.
investigations.earthApp: Fire safety in small sealed environments such as mines, airplanes or submarines.

conditions.note: Same objectives as Saffire-I. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

sensors: solid-state sensors (pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction)
investigations.summary: Third Saffire flight, with extensive instrumentation and data in PSI.

findings.text: Same objectives as Saffire-I: large-scale fire growth and flammability limits.

investigations.spaceApp: A realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which is too risky to test crewed. Results set microgravity flammability limits for spacecraft materials and help validate NASA's material-selection criteria.
investigations.earthApp: Fire safety in small sealed environments such as mines, airplanes or submarines.

fuels: dibutyl phthalate on a porous wick

conditions.note: 30 samples (6 per material) at different airflow rates, heating temperatures and smoke aging times. ISS Expedition 15. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

investigations.summary: Measures the size and distribution of smoke particles from spacecraft materials and evaluates ionization (Shuttle) and photoelectric (ISS) smoke detectors.

findings.text: All samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particles, better detected by an ionization detector; a light-scattering detector would perform very well for most cases.
Arithmetic mean diameters are 100 to 200 nm; for silicone rubber (227 nm) almost half the particle mass is in particles larger than 1000 nm.
The detection target is the early phase (pre-fire heating products), not soot; detectors that measure a wider size spectrum may be more reliable.

investigations.spaceApp: A low-gravity smoke baseline against which future detection technology can be evaluated.
investigations.earthApp: Smoke detectors useful in submarines and underwater laboratories.

conditions.note: Reflight of SAME. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

investigations.summary: Repeats SAME and fixes a problem: the TEM grids came back contaminated and unusable.

findings.text: Quantifies the size liquid smoke droplets reach in low gravity and relates it to smoke generation and transport conditions.
Hypothesis: without buoyancy-driven flows, particle growth by nucleation, condensation and coagulation yields larger particles than in 1 g.

investigations.spaceApp: Technology for an advanced fire detector on long-duration missions.
investigations.earthApp: Smoke detectors developed from SAME/SAME-R can also be useful in submarines or underwater laboratories.

conditions.note: Mitigates the risk of SAME by checking a modified P-Trak particle counter. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

sensors: modified TSI P-Trak (isopropanol condensation and laser counting)
investigations.summary: Checks that a modified P-Trak particle counter works in microgravity; the same instrument used in SAME was used to detect dust.

findings.text: There were concerns the P-Trak would fail in microgravity (isopropanol clogging, or the optics-chamber airflow dynamics).
Contributes to detection systems with higher reliability and sensitivity for extended missions.

investigations.spaceApp: Telling smoke from dust reduces false alarms.
investigations.earthApp: A Shuttle-derived detector (Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector, 1978) already separated smoke from dust in mines.

conditions.note: Its fan-driven flow duct is reused in BASS, BASS-II and SLICE. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

investigations.summary: Studies the smoke point and luminous length of jet flames in coflow, using the duct that BASS and SLICE reuse.

findings.text: Quantifies the sooting propensity of different fuels and the effect of burner diameter and coflow velocity.

investigations.earthApp: Insights toward better fuel formulations and combustion processes, and a better understanding of soot generation.

conditions.note: Uses SPICE hardware. Operated in 2012 per the guide. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

sensors: high-resolution camera (still images with sensor data overlay)
investigations.summary: Structure and lift-off of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

findings.text: Determines lift-off velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters, and the effect of nitrogen dilution.

investigations.earthApp: Numerical models that improve efficiency and cut emissions.

conditions.note: Ground investigation on SPICE data; more than 1600 DSLR images. ASSUMED: O2 21% and 1.013 atm are the ISS standard atmosphere, not stated in the PSI metadata for this investigation.

sensors: color-ratio pyrometry (soot temperature fields from DSLR images)
investigations.summary: Computational and experimental analysis of SPICE data to explain the large discrepancy in soot formation between 1 g and 0 g.

findings.text: Hypothesis: in microgravity flames are longer and more diffuse, with lower temperatures and higher soot concentration than in normal gravity.

investigations.spaceApp: Supports safer fire detection, suppression and cleaner combustion technologies for long-duration missions.
investigations.earthApp: Helps reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency and inform cleaner energy and industrial systems.

upcoming.name: Flammability of Materials on the Moon
upcoming.note: A robotic combustion chamber for the lunar surface on CLPS mission CP-21, planned to launch in late 2026. It will test 21% O2 at 14.7 psia and 34% O2 at 8.2 psia on SIBAL fabric and acrylic rods burned upward and downward. SIBAL burns only downward in lunar gravity in air but extinguishes at once in 1 g (NASA NTRS 20240015307).

upcoming.name: Lunar Combustion Investigation
upcoming.gravity: lunar gravity (1/6 g) by centrifugal acceleration
upcoming.note: Flew on a spinning Blue Origin New Shepard sounding rocket (11 RPM, 1.22 m effective radius). First-ever extended (>25 s) burns in simulated lunar gravity: a cotton-fiberglass fabric and a 4 mm PMMA rod burned together in air at normal pressure for over 2.5 minutes, with oxygen falling until extinction. Results reported in 2025 (NASA NTRS 20250010653); not in PSI.

upcoming.name: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction
upcoming.note: Will test whether NASA-STD-6001's 1-g flame test is conservative in low gravity.

upcoming.name: Flammability Limits at Reduced-g Experiment
upcoming.note: A method to estimate microgravity flammability limits from ground data; a project with JAXA, ESA, CNES and DLR.

environments.name: Lunar base (habitat)
environments.note: 30% O2 or more at 10.2 psi or less (challenge statement). Lunar gravity: no experimental data.

incidents.name: Apollo 1
incidents.text: A flash fire swept the Command Module during a pre-launch test in a 100% oxygen cabin. Grissom, White and Chaffee died. The three-piece hatch took about 90 seconds to open.
incidents.lesson: A unified hatch that opens in 3 seconds, tightly restricted combustible materials and fire-resistant spacesuits.

incidents.name: Apollo 13
incidents.text: Oxygen tank no. 2 exploded en route to the Moon after its heaters overheated and degraded the Teflon insulation; heater voltage had been raised from 28 to 65 V DC without upgrading the thermostats.
incidents.lesson: Oxygen system redesign: a third tank, upgraded thermostats, no stirring fans and stainless-steel-sheathed wiring.

incidents.name: Mir
incidents.text: On 24 February a solid-fuel oxygen generator canister caught fire in the Kvant-1 module. The flame burned for several minutes and the crew fought it with foam extinguishers.
incidents.lesson: Changes to canister preparation and emergency training; the ISS uses dissimilar, redundant oxygen generation.

incidents.name: Artemis II
incidents.text: A smoke alarm sounded about 80,000 miles from Earth, as recounted by the commander in the challenge statement.
incidents.lesson: A reminder of why fast detection and response matter far from home.

spinoffs.name: Firefighter air tank
spinoffs.text: A 20 lb backpack with a 30-minute air supply at 4,500 psi (13 lb lighter than conventional tanks), with an aluminum liner wrapped in glass fibers.

spinoffs.name: Project FIRES: protective clothing
spinoffs.text: Firefighter protective gear using fire-resistant fabrics derived from spacesuit materials, field-tested in 14 municipal fire departments.

spinoffs.name: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector
spinoffs.text: A Space Shuttle detector that tells combustion particles from dust (fewer false alarms) and senses fire before flame and smoke; sensors can be networked for mines.
